Every simulation in these notes runs inline and is seeded, so every render is identical: seed 6376 for the course realization of §7.1 (Stage 1 and the §7.3, §7.4, and §7.6 examples), 6377 for the §7.4 power table, 6378 for Stages 2–3, and 6379 for the §7.5 variance check. Every simulation or data number quoted in the prose is printed by the render from the objects in the code, not typed by hand, so if you change a seed or a setting, those numbers update with the code. Two kinds of statement do not update by themselves: the words around the numbers (a “crossover” or a “rejection” was checked against the render for these seeds, and could need rewording under others), and the forward references in §7.4, which describe §7.8’s results (its rejection on twelve dates, and its check of the h = 1 assumption) in words because they have not yet been computed at that point.

Three Lessons

  1. A combination method is an estimator. Its holdout performance is the population gain from its weights minus the estimation error in them. The weights window is where the estimation error is paid.
  2. The puzzle is a comparison: attainable gain against estimation cost (Smith and Wallis 2009; Claeskens, Magnus, Vasnev and Wang 2016; Wang et al. 2023, §2.6). It bites when the improvement that optimal weights could deliver over equal weights is small relative to the cost of estimating them. Near-equal optimal weights are the important special case — then there is almost nothing to gain — but not the only one: the optimal weights can differ substantially from 1/M1/M and still buy little when the forecasts are largely redundant (Elliott 2011, reviewed in Wang et al. 2023, §2.6; on redundant pools, §2.5). With twelve weights-window observations, the estimation cost is high, which describes most applied work — and Problem Set 3.
  3. Restrictions are a dial between the two. 1/M1/M estimates nothing, inverse-MSE a little, CLS more inside a box, Granger-Ramanathan everything. Moving down the list pays only when the window is long or the gain is large.

The Forecast Combination Puzzle

Stock and Watson (2004) gave it a name: theory says optimally weighted combinations should dominate; in practice, the simple average is very hard to beat. The simulation shows the explanation (Timmermann 2006; Smith and Wallis 2009): the optimal weights have to be estimated, and with short windows the estimation error swamps the gain. The governing comparison is the attainable improvement over equal weights versus the cost of estimating the weights. The most important case in which the gain is small is optimal weights that are near equal, so that there is little to swamp; but it is a special case, not a necessary condition — substantially different optimal weights can still yield little gain when the forecasts are redundant, carrying much the same information (Elliott 2011, reviewed in Wang et al. 2023, §2.6; on redundant pools, §2.5). Enders’ spread example illustrates the near-equal case: his seven forecasts had nearly identical error variances, and on its single forecast date the simple and variance-weighted averages landed closest — one date, so an illustration rather than evidence.

The index fund analogy. Active managers (estimated weights) should beat the index (equal weights) in theory — they pick the winners. In practice, fees eat the edge, and here the fee is estimation error. The index is very hard to beat. But an index fund that holds a bankrupt stock at full weight is not a good index. Equal weights are robust to estimation error, not to a broken member of the pool. Section 7.8 shows what that means on real data.

Looking Ahead — Rolling-Window Combination Weights

Everything here estimated the weights once, on a fixed window. An alternative re-estimates them on a moving window as each holdout date arrives (Stock and Watson 1998), and a related literature lets the weights drift over time (Diebold and Pauly 1987). That trades estimation error — each re-fit uses only the latest window — for adaptivity to structural change: the combination-weight analogue of the fixed-width rolling scheme in §7.2. It is not built in this course. Not assessable.

7.8 The PS3 Workflow on a Series That Isn’t Yours

This is the complete Problem Set 3 workflow, run end to end on UNRATE: Ntotal=N_{\text{total}} = 720 months (1960–2019), T=T = 696 (train ends December 2017), weights window = 2018, holdout = 2019, and the six tracks built in §7.1. The metrics table and the DM test of arima_1 against locf are already done (§7.3 and §7.4). What remains is the combination step.

Step 1: Fit the Four Methods on 2018

ws_un <- list(SA = comb_simple(y_w, F_w), IMSE = comb_inv_mse(y_w, F_w),
              CLS = comb_cls(y_w, F_w),   GR = comb_gr(y_w, F_w))
w_tab <- sapply(ws_un, function(w) c(w0 = w$intercept, w$weights))
round(w_tab, 3)
           SA  IMSE  CLS       GR
w0      0.000 0.000 0.00 -141.450
arima_1 0.167 0.235 0.69    1.224
arima_2 0.167 0.158 0.00   -5.825
arima_3 0.167 0.229 0.00    1.088
locf    0.167 0.179 0.00    5.098
avg_k   0.167 0.198 0.31   -2.605
meanf   0.167 0.001 0.00   24.803
kappa_w <- kappa(cbind(1, F_w), exact = TRUE)   # condition number, GR design matrix
kappa_w
[1] 41619.94

Read across the rows.

  • Inverse-MSE gives meanf a weight of 0.001 — effectively zero — and spreads the rest between 0.16 and 0.24 across the five credible tracks.
  • CLS puts 0.69 on arima_1 and 0.31 on avg_k, and zero everywhere else.
  • Granger-Ramanathan returns an intercept of -141 and a weight of 24.8 on meanf, with large offsetting weights elsewhere. Why? Over twelve months, the expanding mean of more than 696 observations barely moves, so the meanf column is almost a constant — almost collinear with the intercept. The condition number of the regression’s design matrix (intercept plus six tracks; kappa(..., exact = TRUE)) is about 41,620; anything in the thousands means the least-squares solution is extremely sensitive to the data. The regression is trading an enormous intercept against an enormous meanf weight to fit twelve points.

Step 2: Score Everything on 2019

comb_h <- sapply(ws_un, function(w) apply_w(w, F_h))   # N x 4 combined forecasts
rmse_un <- c(apply(F_h, 2, rmse, actual = y_h),
             apply(comb_h, 2, rmse, actual = y_h))
round(rmse_un, 3)
arima_1 arima_2 arima_3    locf   avg_k   meanf      SA    IMSE     CLS      GR 
  0.097   0.097   0.096   0.096   0.108   2.315   0.416   0.093   0.094   0.463

The simple average has a holdout RMSE of 0.416 — roughly four times the credible single tracks’ 0.096 to 0.108. Inverse-MSE (0.093) and CLS (0.094) match or edge out the best single tracks. Granger-Ramanathan (0.463) is worse even than the simple average.

Step 3: Test Each Estimated-Weight Combination Against the Simple Average

Three tests, declared in advance and all reported. We do not pick the holdout winner and then test it on the same twelve dates — that is choosing the hypothesis after seeing the data.

ec_h <- y_h - comb_h
dm_comb <- t(sapply(c("IMSE", "CLS", "GR"), function(m) {
  tst <- dm.test(ec_h[, m], ec_h[, "SA"], h = 1, power = 2)
  c(DM = unname(tst$statistic), p_value = unname(tst$p.value))
}))
signif(dm_comb, 3)
        DM  p_value
IMSE -9.10 1.87e-06
CLS  -9.12 1.83e-06
GR    0.87 4.03e-01

Inverse-MSE against the simple average: DM=\text{DM} = -9.1, p=p = 1.9e-06. CLS: DM=\text{DM} = -9.1, p=p = 1.8e-06. A clear rejection at N=12N = 12 — the §7.4 power lesson from the other side. A gap this large relative to the noise in dtd_t shows up even in twelve months. Granger-Ramanathan against the simple average: p=p = 0.40, no detectable difference. Like every h = 1 result in this module, these pp-values assume that each dtd_t is serially uncorrelated; the Technical Note below checks that assumption, and The Honest Reading reports what it found.

Technical Note — Checking the h = 1 Assumption on dtd_t

The four PS3-design UNRATE tests were run at h = 1: arima_1 against locf (§7.4) and the three combinations against the simple average (above). For each, we look at the autocorrelations of the squared-error loss differential dtd_t at lags 1–3, with a Ljung-Box test of all three, and then re-run the DM test with a Bartlett (Newey-West) variance that allows for serial correlation in dtd_t up to lag h−1h - 1, for h = 2, 3, 4. (We use "bartlett" rather than the default truncated "acf" sum because the truncated sum can turn negative on twelve points, in which case dm.test() warns and falls back to h = 1 (the output then reports horizon 1).)

# The h = 1 DM tests assume d_t is serially uncorrelated. Check it.
dmdep_pairs <- list(                          # (error 1, error 2) for each test
  "arima_1 vs locf" = cbind(e_h[, "arima_1"], e_h[, "locf"]),
  "IMSE vs SA"      = cbind(ec_h[, "IMSE"],   ec_h[, "SA"]),
  "CLS vs SA"       = cbind(ec_h[, "CLS"],    ec_h[, "SA"]),
  "GR vs SA"        = cbind(ec_h[, "GR"],     ec_h[, "SA"]))

# (1) ACF of d_t = e1^2 - e2^2 at lags 1-3, and a Ljung-Box test of all three
dmdep_acf <- t(sapply(dmdep_pairs, function(e) {
  d <- e[, 1]^2 - e[, 2]^2
  r <- acf(d, lag.max = 3, plot = FALSE)$acf[2:4]
  c(lag1 = r[1], lag2 = r[2], lag3 = r[3],
    LB_p = Box.test(d, lag = 3, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)
}))

# (2) Sensitivity: DM p-values with a Bartlett (HAC) variance, lags up to h - 1
dmdep_sens <- t(sapply(dmdep_pairs, function(e) {
  p <- function(h) unname(dm.test(e[, 1], e[, 2], h = h, power = 2,
                                  varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
  c(h1_lag0 = p(1), bartlett_h2 = p(2), bartlett_h3 = p(3), bartlett_h4 = p(4))
}))
stopifnot(all.equal(unname(dmdep_sens[, "h1_lag0"]),        # column 1 reproduces
                    unname(c(dm_un$p.value, dm_comb[, "p_value"]))))  # the tests above
round(dmdep_acf, 3)
                  lag1   lag2   lag3  LB_p
arima_1 vs locf -0.326 -0.113 -0.082 0.580
IMSE vs SA      -0.200 -0.279  0.026 0.587
CLS vs SA       -0.223 -0.253  0.028 0.605
GR vs SA         0.097 -0.047  0.050 0.973
signif(dmdep_sens, 3)
                 h1_lag0 bartlett_h2 bartlett_h3 bartlett_h4
arima_1 vs locf 9.02e-01    8.91e-01    8.85e-01    8.79e-01
IMSE vs SA      1.87e-06    1.54e-06    6.33e-07    6.07e-07
CLS vs SA       1.83e-06    1.30e-06    5.47e-07    5.43e-07
GR vs SA        4.03e-01    4.64e-01    5.07e-01    5.56e-01

Three readings.

  • No autocorrelation is detectable — but twelve points cannot detect much. The Ljung-Box pp-values run from 0.58 to 0.97. The sample autocorrelations are not all small, though: the lag-1 values run from -0.33 to 0.10, and with N=12N = 12 an autocorrelation of that size is well inside the noise. The check is consistent with uncorrelated dtd_t; it does not establish it.
  • The verdicts survive the robust variance. arima_1 against locf has pp between 0.88 and 0.89 across the three Bartlett variances; inverse-MSE and CLS against the simple average stay below 2e-06; Granger-Ramanathan stays between 0.46 and 0.56. None of the four verdicts at 5% changes.
  • Direction. Where the lag-1 autocorrelation is negative, the robust pp-values here came out smaller than the lag-0 ones, so in these data the lag-0 standard error was, if anything, conservative. That is an observation about these four tests, not a theorem — raising h also changes the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold small-sample factor.

Not assessable beyond the Core statement in §7.4: at h = 1, dm.test() assumes serially uncorrelated dtd_t.

The Honest Reading

This is not the textbook story, and the notes would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

  • The simple average did not win, and the reason is not that the estimated weights got lucky. Here the attainable gain over equal weights is large enough to pay for estimating the weights. The pool contains meanf, a forecaster with no business on an I(1) series, and 1/M1/M gives it a sixth of the vote — enough to drag the average about 0.39 percentage points off the actuals every month. Equal weights are robust to estimation error, not to a broken member. Inverse-MSE and CLS won by down-weighting meanf, which is exactly what estimated weights are for: the gain from sidelining one broken member dwarfs the estimation cost of these restricted weights.
  • The tests rest on an assumption about dtd_t, and the check qualifies rather than confirms it. Every DM test here used h = 1, which assumes serially uncorrelated loss differentials. The autocorrelations of the four dtd_t series are not detectably different from zero (Ljung-Box p≥p \ge 0.58), but twelve dates give that check little power; re-running the tests with a serial-correlation-robust variance, no verdict changes (Technical Note above). So the UNRATE verdicts are robust to that check — not definitive.
  • Granger-Ramanathan lost for the Stage 1 reason, amplified by near-collinearity: seven numbers from twelve observations, two of which — the intercept and the nearly constant meanf column — are almost the same regressor.
  • Is estimation the only way to sideline a broken track? That question goes beyond Core; the optional Deeper Dive at the end of this section takes it up.
  • Caveats. One window. 2018–2019 was a calm glide with no turning point, so every credible track had small errors. A different window could rank the methods differently. One realization is one draw; the Monte Carlo of §7.7 is the distribution.

What this means for Problem Set 3. Look at your six tracks before you combine them. If one of them is broken on your series — meanf on an I(1) series is the usual suspect — say so, explain why from the series’ properties, and expect it to drag the simple average. Your scorecard still reports every track and every combination; the reading is where the judgment goes.

Deeper Dive — Robust Combinations on UNRATE

c(simple       = rmse(y_h, rowMeans(F_h)),
  median       = rmse(y_h, apply(F_h, 1, median)),
  trimmed      = rmse(y_h, apply(F_h, 1, function(v) mean(sort(v)[2:5]))),
  simple_five  = rmse(y_h, rowMeans(F_h[, credible])))
     simple      median     trimmed simple_five 
 0.41601502  0.09869660  0.09751126  0.09250425

The median and the trimmed mean (drop the highest and lowest forecast each month) land with the credible tracks, without estimating a single weight: meanf is always the highest forecast, so trimming throws it out. The last entry — a simple average over the five credible tracks — makes the point directly: once the broken member is out of the pool, equal weights are as good as anything else on this window. Not assessable.

Common Pitfalls and Misconceptions

  1. “MASE <1< 1 means my model beat the naive.” No. MASE compares your holdout error with the naive’s training error. The head-to-head on the same dates is U2<1U_2 < 1. On UNRATE 2019, every credible track had MASE at or below 0.71 and U2U_2 between 0.999 and 1.12.
  2. “DM failed to reject, so the models are equally good.” It means the gap is not detectable with these dates. At N=12N = 12, DM rarely detects even a correctly specified estimated model’s advantage over a misspecified one.
  3. “DM always fails with twelve observations.” No. Power depends on the gap relative to the noise in dtd_t. On UNRATE, inverse-MSE against the simple average rejected with p=p = 1.9e-06 at N=12N = 12.
  4. “I can feed residuals(fit) to dm.test().” Out-of-sample forecast errors only. In-sample residuals reward the model that overfits.
  5. “Granger-Ramanathan weights are optimal, so use them.” Optimal in population. With seven parameters from twelve observations, mostly noise: they win the window they were fit on and lose the next one.
  6. “A negative weight is a bug.” It is what unconstrained least squares does with correlated forecasts. It is a warning about estimation error, not an insight about the forecaster. (And an NA weight is exact collinearity — treat it as zero.)
  7. “The simple average always wins.” Not when the pool contains a broken member — meanf on an I(1) series. Equal weights are robust to estimation error, not to a bad forecaster.
  8. “avg_k is a moving-average model.” It is a kk-period average forecast. In this course a moving average is the MA(qq) block, θlϵt−l\theta_l\epsilon_{t-l}.
  9. “Re-fit the ARIMA on y[1:(T+12)] before forecasting the holdout.” Parameters are estimated once, on train; Arima(y, model = fit) reuses them while the information set rolls.
  10. Subsetting a ts with square brackets. y[1:T] drops the frequency; a fresh auto.arima() on it never searches seasonal models. Use window().

Connection to Enders and Other Texts

  • Diebold-Mariano: Enders Chapter 2, Section 9 (“Properties of Forecasts”), eqs. (2.61)–(2.62): the loss differential, the truncated long-run variance, the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold version with a tH−1t_{H-1} reference, the regress-on-a-constant shortcut, and the Clark-McCracken nested-model caveat with the Clark-West adjustment.
  • Combining forecasts: Enders Chapter 2, Section 13, eqs. (2.71)–(2.76): the two-forecast variance, the optimal and inverse-variance weights, the Granger-Ramanathan regression, and the spread example, which illustrates the near-equal-weights case of the puzzle (seven nearly identical error variances); for one forecast date, the simple and variance-weighted averages landed closest, ahead of the regression and SBC (= BIC) weights.

Practice Problems

Core Practice

  1. On the course DGP with a different seed, build the six tracks and report RMSE, MAE, MASE, and U2U_2 on the holdout. Find a track with MASE <1< 1 and U2>1U_2 > 1 (or explain why none exists), and say in one sentence what each of the two numbers means for that track.
  2. On the same realization, run dm.test() for arima_1 against each of the other five tracks. Which differences are significant at 5%? Relate your answer to the size of each RMSE gap.
  3. Re-run the §7.4 power Monte Carlo with power = 1 (absolute loss). Does DM gain or lose power at each NN? Why might it?
  4. Two forecasts have error variances 1 and 4 and error correlation ρ1,2=0.25\rho_{1,2} = 0.25. Compute the optimal two-forecast weight and the combined error variance; compare with the simple average and with the zero-covariance (inverse-variance) weight.
  5. Compute all four combinations on the course DGP with Tw=12T_w = 12 and with Tw=60T_w = 60. Report the weights and the holdout RMSEs. In which case do the Granger-Ramanathan weights look sensible?
  6. On UNRATE, repeat §7.8 with avg_k at k=6k = 6 and k=12k = 12 (use the k argument of tracks_on()). Do the combination rankings change? Justify your choice of kk from the series’ persistence.
  7. Conceptual. A colleague’s Granger-Ramanathan combination has an intercept of -141 and a weight of 25 on one forecast. Explain what produced it, and what you would report instead.
  8. Conceptual. In three to four sentences, explain why the simple average is hard to beat, and name one situation in which it is not. Use the phrase “estimation error” once.

Beyond Core (optional)

  • Re-run the tsCV() Deeper Dive (§7.2) and compare the DM verdict on the ten years of re-estimated origins with the 12-date verdict of §7.4. Why can they differ?
  • Implement Enders’ drop-the-most-negative rule on UNRATE and compare it with CLS.
  • Add the median and trimmed mean to the UNRATE holdout table and test each against the simple average with DM.

Key Takeaways

  1. Many origins, one horizon. The PS3 design estimates each model once and rolls the information set: every forecast is one step ahead, and the three kk-period average forecasts (locf, avg_k, meanf) sit beside three ARIMA tracks.
  2. U2U_2 asks “did you beat the naive here?”; MASE asks “how big was your miss relative to the naive’s typical miss in training?” Report both, and never read MASE <1< 1 as a win.
  3. A metrics table is a ranking, not a verdict. The Diebold-Mariano test is a tt-test on the loss differentials dtd_t, with a standard error that allows for serial correlation; at h = 1, dm.test() uses the lag-0 version, which assumes dtd_t is serially uncorrelated. Whether it rejects depends on the gap relative to the noise in dtd_t — and twelve dates buy little power. On UNRATE 2019 the five credible tracks are descriptively close (RMSE), and the one track-vs-track comparison tested (arima_1 vs locf) does not reject.
  4. Combine because errors diversify. With zero error covariance, the optimal weight is proportional to the inverse error variance.
  5. A combination method is an estimator. With twelve weights-window observations, estimate as little as you can: Granger-Ramanathan’s seven numbers win the window and lose the holdout.
  6. Equal weights are the benchmark to beat — when the pool is sound. The forecast combination puzzle is the cost of estimating the weights outweighing the attainable gain over equal weights — most often because the optimal weights are near equal or the forecasts are redundant. A broken pool member (like meanf on an I(1) series) makes the attainable gain large, so estimated weights (or, see the Deeper Dive, robust ones) can pay for themselves.
  7. Every forecast here used only the series’ own past. Module 8 asks whether another variable can help: the ADL model.

Looking Ahead — Module 8

Look back at what every forecast in this module used: the series’ own past, and nothing else. Three ARIMA models, three averages of past values, and four ways of combining them — and on UNRATE in 2019 the five credible tracks were descriptively close in RMSE, the one track-vs-track comparison tested (arima_1 vs locf, carrying the last value forward) did not reject, and the best combinations only matched the best single tracks’ RMSE. Combinations can only reshuffle the information already in the pool. The combination puzzle hands us a sharper question: what if an exogenous regressor could improve the forecast? Could another variable — initial unemployment-insurance claims, say — carry information that no univariate track has?

Module 8 (ADL Models and Dynamic Multipliers) adds that information directly. It turns on a new slider on the mixing board — βxt\beta x_t and its lags — and asks how a change in xx today works its way into yy over time. The theme of this module was refereeing between univariate forecasts. The theme of the next is letting a second variable into the room.
